specStatements.text: There is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies. The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. This effect is called red-shift.
The observed red-shift provides evidence that space itself (the universe) is expanding and supports the Big Bang theory.
The Big Bang theory suggests that the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense.
Since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.
Students should be able to explain:
• qualitatively the red-shift of light from galaxies that are receding
• that the change of each galaxy’s speed with distance is evidence of an expanding universe
• how red-shift provides evidence for the Big Bang model
• how scientists are able to use observations to arrive at theories such as the Big Bang theory
• that there is still much about the universe that is not understood, for example dark mass and dark energy.

scopeNotes.statement: • qualitatively the red-shift of light from galaxies that are receding
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification asks for a qualitative explanation only, so no numerical treatment of red-shift appears anywhere in this content. There is no formula relating change in wavelength to recession speed, no Hubble relationship of the form speed = constant × distance, and no calculation of a galaxy's speed, distance or age of the universe from a wavelength shift. Every item asks the student to compare shifts as bigger or smaller and to draw the corresponding conclusion about speed and distance in words. Values of wavelength are given only as descriptive comparisons, never as data to be processed into an answer.

scopeNotes.statement: There is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification says most distant galaxies, not all galaxies, and this content keeps that wording. No item states or implies that every object in the sky shows an increased wavelength, and no item introduces blue-shift, which the specification does not name. Where the observation is described, it is described as the specification describes it: an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies.

concepts.definition: The observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies. The light from such a galaxy arrives with a longer wavelength than the same light has when it is produced on Earth, so features in its spectrum appear shifted towards the red end. This effect is called red-shift.

concepts.term: Wavelength and the red end of the spectrum
concepts.definition: Wavelength is the distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave. Within the visible spectrum red light has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest, so an increase in wavelength is described as a shift towards the red end of the spectrum. The word red-shift refers to that direction of shift, not to the colour an object appears.

Moving away from the observer. The observed increase in wavelength of light from most distant galaxies is the evidence that those galaxies are receding from us. The faster a galaxy is receding, the bigger the observed increase in the wavelength of its light.

Each element produces its own characteristic pattern of lines in a spectrum, and that pattern can be produced and measured in a laboratory on Earth. When the same pattern is found in light from a distant galaxy, the whole pattern is observed at longer wavelengths, shifted towards the red end. Comparing the two patterns is how the increase in wavelength is observed.

concepts.term: Link between distance, speed and red-shift
concepts.definition: The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. Distance, recession speed and size of red-shift therefore rise together: a galaxy showing a large red-shift is both further away and moving faster than a galaxy showing a small one.

The observed red-shift provides evidence that space itself (the universe) is expanding. Because every distant galaxy is receding, and recedes faster the further away it is, the galaxies are becoming more widely separated over time. The galaxies are not simply flying outwards through unchanging space away from one special place.

The theory that the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense. If the universe is expanding now, then in the past everything was closer together, which is what this model describes. The observed red-shift supports the Big Bang theory.

concepts.term: Using observations to arrive at a theory
concepts.definition: A scientific theory is an explanation that has to account for what is observed. Scientists observed the red-shift of light from most distant galaxies, and developed the Big Bang theory as a model that explains those observations. When new observations are made, such as those of supernovae from 1998 onwards, the accepted theory has to account for them too, and may be changed.

Since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster. These observations came after the Big Bang theory was already accepted, and they added something the earlier picture did not contain: the recession of distant galaxies is not steady but is speeding up.

Mass in the universe that has not been observed directly. The specification names dark mass as one example of how much about the universe is still not understood, so it is something scientists are aware of but cannot yet fully explain.

The specification names dark energy, alongside dark mass, as an example of something about the universe that is still not understood. Dark mass and dark energy are two different named examples, not two names for one idea, and neither is explained by the Big Bang theory as it currently stands.

misconceptions.question: A distant galaxy shows a large red-shift. Does that mean the galaxy looks red?
misconceptions.correct: No. Red-shift means the wavelength of the light has increased, so features in the spectrum sit closer to the red end than they do in the laboratory.
misconceptions.misconception: Red-shift means the galaxy has turned red, so a strongly red-shifted galaxy is a red one and a galaxy that is not red is not red-shifted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name contains a colour, and the only shift a student has met before is a change of colour, so the term is read as a description of appearance rather than of wavelength.
misconceptions.correction: The evidence for red-shift is the position of lines in a spectrum, not the overall colour. The whole pattern of lines from a known element is found at longer wavelengths than the laboratory pattern, and that shift towards the red end is what the word describes.

misconceptions.question: What does the observed red-shift of most distant galaxies provide evidence for?
misconceptions.correct: It provides evidence that space itself (the universe) is expanding.
misconceptions.misconception: The galaxies were thrown outwards by a huge explosion and are flying away through space that is already there and does not change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name Big Bang suggests a bomb going off in a room, and everyday explosions do throw fragments out through unchanging air.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the red-shift is evidence that space itself (the universe) is expanding. The expansion is of space, not motion of objects through a fixed space, which is why every distant galaxy is observed to be receding.

misconceptions.question: Galaxy B shows a bigger observed increase in wavelength than galaxy A. What does that tell you about B?
misconceptions.correct: Galaxy B is further away than galaxy A and is moving faster than galaxy A.
misconceptions.misconception: A bigger red-shift means a bigger or brighter galaxy, because a large bright galaxy sends more light and so gives a bigger effect.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate a larger measured effect with a larger or brighter source, as they do with loudness and with brightness, and transfer that to a shift in wavelength.
misconceptions.correction: The size of the red-shift depends on how fast the galaxy is receding and therefore on how far away it is. The size and brightness of the galaxy do not appear in the relationship at all.

misconceptions.question: What does the Big Bang theory suggest about how the universe began?
misconceptions.correct: It suggests the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense.
misconceptions.misconception: The Big Bang was an explosion of matter into a huge empty space that was already sitting there waiting to be filled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday meaning of explosion involves material bursting outwards into surrounding space, and diagrams that show a bright point on a black background reinforce the idea of a pre-existing emptiness.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says only that the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense. The red-shift evidence is that space itself is expanding, so space is part of what the theory describes, not a container the universe was placed in.

misconceptions.question: Light from a receding galaxy is red-shifted. Has its wavelength increased or decreased?
misconceptions.correct: It has increased. Red-shift is an observed increase in the wavelength of the light.
misconceptions.misconception: Red-shift means the light is squashed into shorter wavelengths, because the galaxy is being dragged away and the waves are pulled tighter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that a shift happens but not its direction, and the mental picture of something being stretched or squashed is easy to reverse when the wave diagram is not drawn.
misconceptions.correction: Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum, so a shift towards the red end must be an increase in wavelength. The specification defines red-shift as an observed increase in wavelength.

misconceptions.question: What do observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards suggest about distant galaxies?
misconceptions.correct: They suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.
misconceptions.misconception: The supernova observations showed that the expansion is running out of energy, so distant galaxies are gradually slowing down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everything a student has seen thrown or fired slows down afterwards, so a universe that started with a bang is expected to be losing speed rather than gaining it.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states the opposite: since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster. That is why the observations mattered enough to change the accepted picture.

misconceptions.question: How well do scientists understand dark mass and dark energy?
misconceptions.correct: They do not. There is still much about the universe that is not understood, and dark mass and dark energy are the examples given.
misconceptions.misconception: Dark mass and dark energy are fully explained parts of the Big Bang theory, and scientists have already worked out what they are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two ideas are named confidently in textbooks and documentaries, and being named makes them sound settled rather than open.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names them precisely as examples of what is not understood. Naming something is not the same as explaining it, and a correct answer must say that these remain unexplained.

misconceptions.question: How were scientists able to arrive at a theory such as the Big Bang theory?
misconceptions.correct: They made observations, including the red-shift of light from most distant galaxies, and developed a theory that explains those observations.
misconceptions.misconception: The Big Bang is just somebody's guess about the past, because nobody was there to see it and it cannot be tested.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday word theory means a hunch, and an event long before any observer seems to be beyond the reach of evidence.
misconceptions.correction: A scientific theory has to account for observations that can be made now. The red-shift of light from distant galaxies is observed today, and any theory of the universe has to explain it; that is how observations lead to theories.

misconceptions.question: Two galaxies are receding. Which one is moving faster, the nearer one or the more distant one?
misconceptions.correct: The more distant one. The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving.
misconceptions.misconception: The nearer galaxies must be the fast ones, because things slow down the further they travel and the distant ones have gone furthest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday objects lose speed with distance travelled, so a student applies that pattern and inverts the relationship the specification actually states.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states the relationship directly: the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. Distance and speed increase together.

misconceptions.question: Does the observed red-shift prove that the Big Bang theory is true?
misconceptions.correct: No. It provides evidence that supports the theory, and the theory can still be changed by new observations.
misconceptions.misconception: Red-shift proves the Big Bang, so the theory is now a fact and no new evidence could ever alter it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat strong supporting evidence as final proof, and school science is often presented as a list of settled answers rather than as models held up by evidence.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the red-shift supports the Big Bang theory. The supernova observations from 1998 onwards show how a theory can be added to when new evidence appears, and dark mass and dark energy show how much is still unexplained.

misconceptions.question: Every distant galaxy we observe is receding from us. Does that put the Earth at the centre of the universe?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is the evidence that space itself is expanding, which makes every galaxy recede from every other galaxy.
misconceptions.misconception: If everything is moving away from us in every direction, then we must be standing at the centre of the explosion that started it all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The observation really is that things recede from us in all directions, and the only everyday situation that produces that pattern is standing at the middle of something blowing apart.
misconceptions.correction: Because space itself is expanding, an observer in any galaxy would see the same thing: all the other galaxies receding, and the distant ones receding fastest. The observation therefore identifies no centre at all.

misconceptions.question: Are dark mass and dark energy two names for the same thing?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are two separate examples the specification gives of what is still not understood about the universe.
misconceptions.misconception: Dark mass and dark energy both mean the invisible stuff out in space, so the two terms can be swapped over freely.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both terms begin with dark and both stand for something unseen, so they blur together in memory as one vague idea.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists them separately, as two examples. Mass and energy are different physical quantities and the terms must not be exchanged in an answer.

misconceptions.question: Why is the wavelength of light from a distant galaxy observed to be longer than in the laboratory?
misconceptions.correct: Because the galaxy is receding, so the light waves reaching us are stretched out to a longer wavelength.
misconceptions.misconception: The light slows down over such an enormous journey, and slower light must have a longer wavelength by the time it arrives.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the idea that a moving object loses speed over a long journey to light, and then reach for the wave equation to link a lower speed to a longer wavelength.
misconceptions.correction: The observed increase in wavelength is linked to the recession of the galaxy, not to the light tiring on the way. The bigger the red-shift, the faster the galaxy is moving and the further away it is.

misconceptions.question: What sort of event does the Big Bang theory describe?
misconceptions.correct: It describes the universe beginning from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense.
misconceptions.misconception: The Big Bang was an enormous star that blew up, in the same way that a supernova is a star exploding.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Supernovae are mentioned in the same short section of the specification, and both ideas involve something violent and bright, so the two are merged into one story.
misconceptions.correction: The Big Bang theory is about the beginning of the whole universe from a very small, extremely hot and dense region. Supernovae are separate objects observed since 1998 onwards, whose light tells us how distant galaxies are receding.

misconceptions.question: Which observations first led scientists to the Big Bang theory?
misconceptions.correct: The observed red-shift of light from most distant galaxies, which is evidence that the universe is expanding.
misconceptions.misconception: The Big Bang theory came from the supernova observations made since 1998 onwards, since those are the observations named with a date.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The date 1998 is the only date in the section, so it is remembered as the moment the whole theory was worked out.
misconceptions.correction: Red-shift is the evidence that the universe is expanding and that supports the Big Bang theory. The supernova observations came later and added something further: that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.

misconceptions.question: A galaxy is observed to be red-shifted. Is it moving towards us or away from us?
misconceptions.correct: Away from us. Red-shift is observed in light from galaxies that are receding.
misconceptions.misconception: A galaxy coming towards us would push its light waves out in front of it and stretch them, so an increased wavelength means it is approaching.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The idea of a wave being pushed ahead of a moving source sounds like stretching, and without a clear diagram the direction of the effect is guessed.
misconceptions.correction: The specification links the increase in wavelength to galaxies that are receding. The waves are stretched because the source is moving away while the light travels.

misconceptions.question: Could the red-shift of light from distant galaxies be caused by dust in space?
misconceptions.correct: No. The increase in wavelength is evidence that the galaxies are receding and that space itself is expanding.
misconceptions.misconception: The light passes through dust on its long journey and loses energy, which reddens it in the way a sunset is reddened.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that the setting Sun looks red because of the atmosphere, and offer the same explanation for anything described as red.
misconceptions.correction: Red-shift is identified by the whole pattern of spectral lines appearing at longer wavelengths, and the size of that shift is larger for the more distant, faster galaxies. That systematic link to distance and speed is what makes it evidence of an expanding universe.

misconceptions.question: A galaxy shows a very large red-shift. What can you say about its distance?
misconceptions.correct: It is one of the more distant galaxies, because the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the red-shift.
misconceptions.misconception: Red-shift only tells you how fast a galaxy is moving; how far away it is has to be measured in some completely separate way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Speed feels like the direct cause of the shift, so distance is treated as an unrelated piece of information rather than as part of the same relationship.
misconceptions.correction: The specification ties the three together: the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. A large red-shift therefore indicates both a high speed and a large distance.

mcqs.stem: Light from a distant galaxy is compared with light from the same element produced in a laboratory on Earth. What is observed about the light from the galaxy?

options.text: Its wavelength has increased
options.rationale: Red-shift is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies.

options.text: Its wavelength has decreased
options.rationale: A student who recalls that a shift occurs but not its direction picks the opposite change.

options.text: Its colour has turned red
options.rationale: The word red in red-shift is read as a description of the colour the galaxy appears.

options.text: Its speed has decreased
options.rationale: A student who thinks light tires over a long journey expects it to arrive travelling more slowly.

mcqs.stem: The light from galaxy B shows a bigger observed increase in wavelength than the light from galaxy A. What can be concluded about galaxy B?

options.text: It is closer to us than A and moving faster than A
options.rationale: A student who links red-shift to speed alone reads the bigger shift as speed and guesses the distance.

options.text: It is further away than A and moving faster than A
options.rationale: The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength.

options.text: It is a larger and brighter galaxy than galaxy A is
options.rationale: A bigger measured effect is assumed to come from a bigger, brighter source.

options.text: It is further away than A and moving slower than A
options.rationale: A student who expects things to slow down over distance inverts the speed–distance relationship.

mcqs.stem: The light from most distant galaxies shows red-shift. What does this observation provide evidence for?

options.text: That galaxies fly outwards through fixed space
options.rationale: The Big Bang is pictured as a bomb throwing fragments through space that already exists.

options.text: That the Earth sits at the centre of everything
options.rationale: Recession observed in every direction is taken to mean we occupy a special central position.

options.text: That space itself (the universe) is expanding
options.rationale: The specification states that the observed red-shift is evidence that space itself (the universe) is expanding.

options.text: That the universe is shrinking back to a point
options.rationale: A student who reverses the direction of the shift concludes the galaxies are approaching.

mcqs.stem: According to the Big Bang theory, how did the universe begin?

options.text: As an explosion of matter into a huge space already there
options.rationale: The everyday meaning of explosion supplies a pre-existing empty space to expand into.

options.text: From a very large region that was extremely cold and thin
options.rationale: A student who recalls the structure of the sentence but not the words reverses every term in it.

options.text: When a very large star collapsed and then blew itself apart
options.rationale: Supernovae are named in the same section, so the two events are merged into one.

options.text: From a very small region that was extremely hot and dense
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification says the Big Bang theory suggests.

mcqs.stem: What do observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards suggest about distant galaxies?

options.text: They are receding from us ever faster
options.rationale: Since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.

options.text: They are receding but are slowing down
options.rationale: An expansion that started with a bang is expected to lose speed, as thrown objects do.

options.text: They have stopped receding from us
options.rationale: The same expectation of slowing, taken to its end point, suggests the expansion has halted.

options.text: They are now moving back towards us
options.rationale: A student unsure which direction red-shift indicates reads the newer evidence as approach.

mcqs.stem: Every distant galaxy is observed to be receding, and the further away a galaxy is the faster it recedes. Why is this evidence of an expanding universe?

options.text: We are at the centre of the explosion, so everything else moves away from us
options.rationale: Recession in all directions is taken as proof of a central position rather than of expansion.

options.text: Space itself is stretching, so galaxies separate faster the further apart they are
options.rationale: A uniform expansion of space makes every galaxy recede, with the most distant receding fastest.

options.text: The galaxies were thrown outwards through space and have never slowed since
options.rationale: The Big Bang is treated as an ordinary explosion inside a space that does not change.

options.text: The nearest galaxies recede fastest, so the outer edge is being left behind
options.rationale: A student who inverts the speed–distance relationship builds an explanation around it.

mcqs.stem: How does the observed red-shift provide evidence for the Big Bang model?

options.text: Red-shift proves that the Big Bang happened, so no other model can now be tested
options.rationale: Supporting evidence is treated as final proof that closes the question for good.

options.text: The red glow we detect is the flash of the explosion still on its way to us
options.rationale: The Big Bang is pictured as a fireball whose light is still arriving from a distant place.

options.text: Galaxies are separating now, so in the past matter was in a far smaller, denser region
options.rationale: Running an expanding universe backwards leads to the very small, extremely hot and dense region the theory describes.

options.text: Red-shift shows the galaxies are burning out, so the universe must have begun
options.rationale: The colour word is linked to stars cooling and ageing rather than to a change of wavelength.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes how scientists were able to use observations to arrive at the Big Bang theory?

options.text: They decided what the theory should say, then looked for facts that would fit it
options.rationale: Theory is read in its everyday sense of a hunch that is defended rather than tested.

options.text: They proved the theory by an experiment, so it can never be altered by anyone
options.rationale: School science can look like a set of proved facts rather than models supported by evidence.

options.text: They based the theory on the supernovae observed since 1998 onwards, and no other
options.rationale: The only date in the section is remembered as the origin of the whole theory.

options.text: They observed the red-shift of distant galaxies and built a theory that explains it
options.rationale: A theory is developed to account for observations that can be made, and red-shift is that observation.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about dark mass and dark energy matches the specification?

options.text: They are examples of what is still not understood about the universe
options.rationale: The specification names them as examples of how much about the universe is not understood.

options.text: They are fully explained by the Big Bang theory as it currently stands
options.rationale: Being confidently named makes the two ideas sound like settled parts of the theory.

options.text: They are two different names used by scientists for the very same thing
options.rationale: Both terms begin with dark and stand for something unseen, so they blur together.

options.text: They are the dark lines seen in the spectra of the most distant galaxies
options.rationale: The word dark is attached to the spectral lines used to observe red-shift.

mcqs.stem: The pattern of lines in the spectrum of a distant galaxy is compared with the pattern produced by the same element in a laboratory. The galaxy's lines are all found closer to the red end. What does this show?

options.text: The wavelength has decreased, so the galaxy is receding from us
options.rationale: The recession is recalled correctly but the direction of the wavelength change is reversed.

options.text: The wavelength has increased, so the galaxy is receding from us
options.rationale: A shift towards the red end is an increase in wavelength, observed in light from galaxies that are receding.

options.text: The wavelength has increased, so the galaxy is approaching us
options.rationale: The stretching of the waves is wrongly attributed to a source moving towards the observer.

options.text: The galaxy is made of red-hot gas rather than the element used
options.rationale: Red-shift is read as a statement about the colour and temperature of the source.

mcqs.stem: Light from galaxies X, Y and Z is examined. X shows a small increase in wavelength, Y a medium increase and Z a large increase. Which galaxy is furthest away, and which is moving fastest?

options.text: X is furthest away and X is moving fastest
options.rationale: A student who thinks distant objects have slowed reverses the whole ordering.

options.text: Z is furthest away and X is moving fastest
options.rationale: Distance and speed are treated as unconnected quantities that need separate reasoning.

options.text: Z is furthest away and Z is moving fastest
options.rationale: The bigger the observed increase in wavelength, the faster the galaxy moves and the further away it is.

options.text: X is furthest away and Z is moving fastest
options.rationale: The shift is linked to speed only, leaving distance to be assigned the other way round.

mcqs.stem: The supernova observations made since 1998 onwards changed what scientists say about the expansion of the universe. What does this show about scientific theories?

options.text: Once a theory is accepted new observations cannot alter it
options.rationale: An accepted theory is treated as a proved fact that later evidence cannot touch.

options.text: New observations showed the expansion has been slowing down
options.rationale: The supernova evidence is reversed to fit the expectation that expansion loses speed.

options.text: New observations replaced red-shift as evidence of expansion
options.rationale: The dated observations are assumed to have taken over from the original evidence.

options.text: New observations can change what an accepted theory says
options.rationale: Theories must account for the observations available, so new evidence can revise an accepted model.

mcqs.stem: Explain qualitatively why light from a galaxy that is receding is observed with a longer wavelength than the same light produced on Earth.

options.text: The galaxy moves away as the light travels, so the waves reach us stretched out
options.rationale: Recession of the source while the light is emitted increases the observed wavelength; this is red-shift.

options.text: The light slows down on its long journey, so its waves are longer on arrival
options.rationale: Light is expected to lose speed over distance in the way an everyday moving object does.

options.text: The light loses energy in dust in space, which reddens it as a sunset is reddened
options.rationale: The familiar explanation for a red sunset is offered for anything described as red.

options.text: The galaxy moves away from us, which squashes the waves to a shorter wavelength
options.rationale: The motion is correct but the effect on wavelength is reversed.
